DCS IO Allocation: Rules for Assigning I/O to Cards and Racks, Redundant Transmitter Separation, Spare Capacity and a Card Count Calculator

Good I/O allocation decides whether one failed card trips a whole unit or only raises an alarm. This page walks through the rules engineers use to spread redundant signals, group by unit, size spares and count cards with a calculator.

Redundant Separation 1oo2 and 2oo3 Inputs Signal Type Grouping Spare Capacity Card Calculator

DCS IO allocation is the job of mapping every field signal in the IO list to a controller, rack, card and channel. Learn the separation rules for redundant transmitters, grouping by unit and signal type, spare sizing and a card count calculator.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn dcs io allocation, the rules for assigning every field signal to the right controller, rack, card and channel.

What Is DCS IO Allocation?

DCS IO allocation is the design step where every signal in the IO list is assigned to a specific controller, rack, I/O card and channel. It follows fixed rules so that redundant signals sit on different hardware, each process unit stays together and enough spare capacity remains for future loops.

Quick Answer
  • Put duplex and triplex transmitters on different cards, and preferably different racks and power supplies
  • Group signals by process unit so one controller failure affects only one unit
  • Keep AI, AO, DI, DO, HART and intrinsically safe circuits on their own card types
  • Plan 20 to 30 % installed spare channels plus empty slots for new cards
  • Count cards from points times spare factor, divided by channels per card, rounded up

Allocation starts only after the instrument IO list is frozen, because every row in that list becomes one channel. If you need a refresher on how the system itself is built, read our guide to the distributed control system before going further.

Control Global explains that in traditional marshalling the field wiring lands on terminal blocks and each pair is then cross wired by hand to the right I/O card and controller. Every one of those cross wires is a decision made during allocation, so a bad allocation becomes expensive rewiring later.

DCS IO Allocation Rules for Cards and Racks

Most EPC contractors follow a similar rule set for DCS IO allocation, applied in the order below.

1
Split by system
Separate BPCS and SIS signals first, since IEC 61511 expects independent safety hardware.
2
Split by process unit
Give each unit its own controller or card group so a fault stays local.
3
Split by signal type
Match AI, AO, DI, DO, RTD and thermocouple points to card types.
4
Separate redundant signals
Place A, B and C transmitters of one measurement on different cards, racks and power feeds.
5
Keep loops together
Put the PV and the valve output of one control loop in the same controller to avoid peer to peer delays.
6
Add spares
Leave installed spare channels on each card and empty slots in each rack.
7
Check loading
Verify CPU load, memory and card power budget before freezing.

Zero Instrument notes that signals for one piece of equipment, such as a pump start, stop, run feedback and trip status, should stay in the same controller or cabinet. This keeps interlock logic local and makes loop checks and DCS commissioning far simpler.

Do You Know?

Emerson states in its DeltaV IS electronic marshalling data sheet that one CHARM I/O card handles 96 channels across 8 baseplates of 12 CHARMs. The same data sheet says each channel can have its own individually defined signal type.

How to Separate Redundant Transmitters

The main purpose of DCS IO allocation for redundant instruments is simple: no single card, rack, power supply or cable should be able to take out more than one leg of the measurement. If two pressure transmitters on the same header share one AI card, a card failure removes both and the redundancy you paid for is gone.

ArrangementMinimum RuleBetter Practice
Duplex AI (1oo2 or 2oo2)A and B on different cardsDifferent racks and power supplies
Triplex AI (2oo3)A, B and C on three cardsThree racks or three I/O nodes
Redundant control valve outputTwo AO channels on two cardsRedundant AO card pair

Our article on 2oo3 voting logic shows why a single shared card turns a triplex trip into a common cause failure. The same thinking applies to the broader family of voting architectures, where the logic is only as good as the independence of its inputs.

Quick Tip

When you separate A and B transmitters, also separate their multicore cables and junction boxes. A single damaged cable tray can otherwise defeat perfect card allocation.

Signal Type Separation: AI, AO, DI, DO, HART and IS

Card types are built for one family of signals, so DCS IO allocation always groups points by type before anything else. A quick review of AI, AO, DI and DO signals helps when you sort the IO list into these groups.

AI HART

4 to 20 mA transmitter inputs with HART diagnostics.

Best for: Pressure, flow, level transmitters
Analog
AO HART

4 to 20 mA outputs to positioners and drives.

Best for: Control valves, VFD setpoints
Analog
DI 24 V DC

Dry contacts and NAMUR sensors for status.

Best for: Valve feedback, motor run status
Discrete
DO 24 V DC

Powered or relay outputs for solenoids and motors.

Best for: Solenoid valves, start commands
Discrete
RTD and TC

Low level temperature inputs with linearisation.

Best for: Bearing and process temperatures
Low Level
Intrinsically Safe

Energy limited channels for Zone 0 and Zone 1 devices.

Best for: Hazardous area instruments
IS

Zero Instrument also advises keeping signals with different power types, such as 24 V DC and 230 V AC, on separate modules to avoid interference. HART capable cards matter if you want asset management, and our guide on how the HART protocol works explains what that extra channel carries.

Intrinsic Safety Rule
Never mix IS and non IS wiring on the same terminal strip or card unless the hardware is certified for it. Keep 50 mm separation or a partition as required by IEC 60079 14 and your hazardous area dossier.

How Much Spare I/O Should a DCS Have?

There is no single standard number, and engineers in a Control Design survey gave answers from 5 to 25 %. A Siemens engineer quoted there called 20 % the generally recommended spare, with 10 % as the lowest he would accept.

15 to 20 %Spare AI and AO channels suggested by Zero Instrument
10 to 15 %Spare DI and DO channels suggested by Zero Instrument
50 %Controller CPU load limit during FAT in the same guidance
96Channels per CHARM I/O card, per Emerson

Many project teams settle on 20 to 30 % for DCS IO allocation, counting installed spare channels plus empty slots for future cards. Always follow the client design basis first, since spare philosophy is a commercial decision as well as a technical one.

Generous Spare (25 to 30 %)
  • Easy to add loops during commissioning
  • Absorbs late IO list changes
  • Leaves room for plant debottlenecking
Tight Spare (10 % or less)
  • Lower hardware cost at purchase
  • Smaller cabinets and footprint
  • Expensive new racks for any expansion

Card Count Calculation With Spare Percentage

The calculator below does the DCS IO allocation card count for one signal type. Enter the used points, channels per card, spare percentage and 1 for simplex or 2 for redundant card pairs.

Card Count Calculator
Result
Required channels 225, cards needed 15, modules to buy 15, installed channels 240, real spare 60 channels (33.3 % of used points)
Solved example: 180 AI points, 16 channel cards, 25 % spare
Required channels = 180 × 1.25 = 225
Cards = 225 ÷ 16 = 14.06, round up
Cards needed = 15
Installed channels = 15 × 16 = 240
Real spare = 240 minus 180 = 60 channels
Real spare = 33.3 % of used points

Rounding up to whole cards gives more spare than you asked for, so the real spare here is 33.3 % and not 25 %. Run the calculation once per signal type.

For a quick check on transmitter loops on those cards, our HART loop voltage budget calculator confirms that each 4 to 20 mA loop still has enough voltage after barriers and cable resistance.

Marshalling Cabinet vs Electronic Marshalling

In a classic system, field multicores land in a marshalling cabinet and jumper wires connect each terminal to the allocated card channel in the system cabinet. With electronic marshalling, the field pair lands on any free terminal and the channel is assigned to a controller in software.

Traditional Cross Wiring
  • Allocation must be fixed before cabinet build
  • Late IO list changes mean rewiring
  • Separate IS barriers and marshalling panels
Electronic Marshalling (CHARMs style)
  • Any channel can serve any controller
  • Signal type set by a plug in module
  • Fewer cabinets and no cross wires

Emerson states in its DeltaV electronic marshalling data sheet that a CHARM I/O card can serve up to 4 controllers and that no cross wiring is required.

PDF
DeltaV IS Electronic Marshalling Product Data Sheet
Emerson PDF covering CHARM I/O card capacity, IS CHARM types and redundancy

Electronic marshalling does not cancel DCS IO allocation separation rules, because two CHARMs on one baseplate still share a carrier. Keep duplex and triplex inputs on different CHARM I/O cards, and read how remote and distributed I/O changes the cabinet layout.

IO List Columns Needed for Allocation

A DCS IO allocation sheet is just the IO list with hardware columns added. The table shows the minimum set that most projects use, which also feeds the instrument loop diagram and the cable schedule.

ColumnExampleWhy It Matters
Tag numberPT 1101ALinks to instrument index
ServiceReactor feed pressure AShows redundant partner
Signal typeAI HART 2 wireSelects card type
SystemBPCS or SISKeeps safety separate
Hazardous areaZone 1, ISSelects IS channel
Controller / RackCTL 01 / R2Unit grouping check
Card / ChannelSlot 5 / Ch 07Wiring and loop check
JB and multicoreJB 11 / MC 11 03Cable separation check
Redundancy groupPT 1101 A, B, CCard separation check

The tag column must match the instrument index exactly, otherwise the allocation and wiring documents drift apart during revisions.

Myth: Controller redundancy means I/O redundancy
Fact: A redundant controller pair still reads simplex cards unless redundant I/O is bought separately
Myth: Spare channels scattered across cards are enough
Fact: A full spare card per type is easier to use and avoids fragmented wiring
Myth: Electronic marshalling removes the need for allocation rules
Fact: Separation of redundant legs still applies at the CHARM I/O card and carrier level
Myth: Grouping by signal type alone is fine
Fact: Grouping by unit first limits how much plant one hardware fault can stop

Common DCS IO Allocation Mistakes

Symptom in PlantLikely Allocation CauseFix
Both level legs fail togetherA and B on one AI cardMove B to another rack
Whole unit trips on one card faultUnits mixed on shared cardsRegroup by unit at next shutdown
Slow loop responsePV and output in different controllersKeep loop in one controller
No room for new pumpNo installed spare or slotsAdd remote I/O node
Noise on AI channelsAC and DC signals on shared cableSeparate cables and cards
Quick Tip

Print the allocation sorted by card and highlight every redundancy group in a different colour. Any card with two highlights of the same colour is a separation error.

Do You Know?

Emerson describes each CHARM as having current limiting and a fail open design, so a fault on one channel is isolated from its neighbours.

  • BPCS and SIS points on separate hardware
  • Redundant legs on different cards, racks and power supplies
  • Each process unit grouped in its own controller or card group
  • Control loop PV and output in the same controller
  • IS circuits on IS channels with segregated wiring
  • 20 to 30 % installed spare and empty rack slots
  • Controller CPU load below 50 % at FAT
  • Allocation sheet tags match the instrument index

Use this DCS IO allocation checklist again during the DCS FAT and SAT, because late IO list changes often break the original separation.

DCS IO Allocation FAQ

What is IO allocation in DCS?

DCS IO allocation is the process of assigning every field signal from the IO list to a controller, rack, card and channel. It is done after the IO list is frozen and before cabinet drawings are released.

The allocation follows rules for redundancy, unit grouping, signal type and spare capacity. A good allocation sheet becomes the base document for wiring, loop diagrams and loop checks.

How much spare I/O should be kept in a DCS?

Most projects keep 20 % installed spare channels and extra empty slots for future cards. Guidance from vendors and experts ranges from about 10 % to 30 % depending on project size.

Zero Instrument suggests 15 to 20 % for analog channels and 10 to 15 % for discrete channels. Always follow the client design basis, because spare capacity affects both cost and future expansion.

Why should redundant transmitters be on different I/O cards?

If two redundant transmitters share one card, a single card failure removes both readings at once. That turns a redundant measurement into a single point of failure for control or trip logic.

Putting each leg on its own card, rack and power supply keeps at least one healthy reading. The same rule applies to 2oo3 voting where three legs need three separate cards.

What is the difference between a marshalling cabinet and a system cabinet?

A marshalling cabinet receives field multicores and provides terminals, barriers and cross wiring to sort the signals. The system cabinet holds the controllers, I/O cards and power supplies that process those signals.

Cross wiring between the two cabinets follows the allocation sheet channel by channel. Electronic marshalling designs reduce or remove this cross wiring because channels are assigned in software.

Should control loop input and output be on the same controller?

Yes, the measured value and the valve output of one control loop should sit in the same controller. This avoids delays and extra failure points from peer to peer communication between controllers.

The input and output can be on different cards inside that controller without any problem. Only cascade or plant wide strategies normally need signals shared between controllers over the network.
